title: Problem Overview
content:
**Erdős Problem #328: Partitioning Sets with Bounded Representation Function**

Can sets with bounded convolution $r_A \leq C$ be partitioned so each piece has $r < C$?

**DISPROVED** by Nešetřil-Rödl (1985): NO for all $C$, even with arbitrarily many pieces.

Originally posed by Erdős and Donald J. Newman [ErGr80, p.48].
mathContext: The problem connects the convolution $\mathbf{1}_A * \mathbf{1}_A$ to Ramsey-type partition questions. The representation function $r_A(n) = |\{(a,b) \in A^2 : a+b=n\}|$ is the self-convolution evaluated at $n$. Erdős and Newman asked whether this quantity can always be reduced by partitioning—the answer is fundamentally no.

title: Imports and Namespace
content: Imports `Nat.Basic`, `Set.Basic`, `Finset.Basic`, and `BigOperators` from Mathlib. The `Erdos328` namespace encapsulates all definitions and results.
mathContext: The formalization uses both `Set ℕ` (for infinite sets in the theoretical statements) and `Finset ℕ` (for computational definitions like `rA`). BigOperators provides summation notation over finite sets.

title: representationFunction
content:
**representationFunction A n** counts ordered pairs $(a,b) \in A \times A$ with $a+b=n$:
$$r_A(n) = |\{(a,b) \in A^2 : a+b = n\}|$$

Implemented by filtering `Finset.range(n+1) × Finset.range(n+1)` for pairs in $A$ summing to $n$.
mathContext: This is the self-convolution $\mathbf{1}_A * \mathbf{1}_A(n)$. For Sidon sets, $r_A(n) \leq 2$ for all $n$. The function counts ordered pairs, so $r_A(2a) \geq 1$ whenever $a \in A$ (from the pair $(a,a)$). The additive energy $E(A) = \sum_n r_A(n)^2$ is a related quantity central to additive combinatorics.

title: rA (Finset version)
content: **rA A n** provides an alternative computation of the representation count on `Finset ℕ`. Filters elements $a \in A$ with $a \leq n$ and $n-a \in A$.
mathContext: This definition counts the number of elements $a \in A$ such that $n-a$ also belongs to $A$, which equals the number of representations $n = a + b$ with $a,b \in A$ (where $b = n-a$). This is computationally simpler than the product-based definition.

title: hasBoundedConvolution
content: **hasBoundedConvolution A C**: the set $A$ satisfies $r_A(n) \leq C$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This captures the notion of an 'additively thin' set—one where no integer has too many representations as a sum from $A$.
mathContext: Sets with bounded convolution form a natural hierarchy indexed by $C$. At $C=0$: only the empty set. At $C=1$: unique-sum sets (very sparse). At $C=2$: Sidon sets. The Erdős-Turán conjecture asks whether $r_A$ can be bounded if $A$ is an asymptotic basis of order 2.

title: isSidonSet
content:
**isSidonSet A**: all pairwise sums are distinct—if $a+b = c+d$ with $a,b,c,d \in A$, then $\{a,b\} = \{c,d\}$. Equivalently, $r_A(n) \leq 2$ for all $n$.

Named after Simon Sidon, who studied these sets in connection with Fourier analysis on groups (1932).
mathContext: Sidon sets (also called $B_2$ sets) are fundamental in additive combinatorics. Erdős and Turán (1941) proved $|A \cap [1,N]| \leq \sqrt{N} + O(N^{1/4})$. The current best construction (Ruzsa 1998, building on Singer 1938) gives $|A \cap [1,N]| \geq \sqrt{N} - O(N^{5/16})$. The exact maximum size remains a major open problem.

title: isBhSet
content: **isBhSet A h**: $A$ is a $B_h$ set, meaning all $h$-wise sums are distinct (up to permutation). Defined here as `hasBoundedConvolution A (h!)`, which is a sufficient but not equivalent condition.
mathContext: $B_h$ sets generalize Sidon sets to $h$-fold sums. For $B_h$ sets, $|A \cap [1,N]| = O(N^{1/h})$. The Erdős-Turán conjecture for $B_h$ sets remains open for all $h \geq 2$. Note: the formalization uses $h!$ as bound, which is conservative; the true bound for $B_h$ is $h!$ for ordered representations.

title: sidon_bounded_convolution
content:
**sidon_bounded_convolution**: If $A$ is a Sidon set, then $r_A(n) \leq 2$ for all $n$.

This follows directly from the definition: in a Sidon set, each $n$ has at most one unordered pair $\{a,b\}$ with $a+b=n$, giving at most 2 ordered pairs.
mathContext: The bound $r_A \leq 2$ is tight: $r_A(2a) = 1$ for $a \in A$ (the pair $(a,a)$), and $r_A(a+b) = 2$ for distinct $a,b \in A$. The axiom bridges the 'all sums distinct' definition with the convolution bound.

title: isPartition
content: **isPartition A parts**: a formal partition of set $A$ into pieces $A_1, \ldots, A_t$. Requires: (1) every $x \in A$ belongs to exactly one piece, (2) every piece is a subset of $A$.
mathContext: The partition is represented as `List (Set ℕ)` rather than a function from an index type. The uniqueness condition (exactly one piece) ensures disjointness: $A_i \cap A_j = \emptyset$ for $i \neq j$.

title: hasStrictlySmaller
content: **hasStrictlySmaller parts C**: each partition piece $A_i$ satisfies $r_{A_i}(n) < C$ for all $n$. This is the 'improvement' condition: partitioning should reduce the maximum representation from $\leq C$ to $< C$.
mathContext: The strict inequality $< C$ (rather than $\leq C-1$) is key: even reducing by 1 is impossible. For $C=2$ (Sidon sets), this asks whether we can partition into unique-sum sets ($r \leq 1$).

title: erdos_newman_question
content:
**erdos_newman_question**: the formal statement of the Erdős-Newman conjecture.
$$\forall C, \exists t(C), \forall A \text{ with } r_A \leq C, \exists \text{partition into } \leq t \text{ pieces with } r_{A_i} < C$$

The key feature: $t$ depends only on $C$, not on $A$.
mathContext: This is a 'uniform' partition question: the number of pieces $t$ must work for ALL sets with the same bound $C$. Even the weaker question where $t$ depends on $A$ (formalized as `nesetril_rodl_strong`) has a negative answer.

title: erdos_C3_counterexample
content:
**erdos_C3_counterexample** (Erdős 1980): There exists a set $A$ with $r_A \leq 3$ that cannot be partitioned into pieces with $r < 3$, no matter how many pieces are used.

This was Erdős's first partial result toward Problem #328.
mathContext: Erdős [Er80e] constructed explicit examples for $C=3$ and $C=4$, and showed the answer is NO for infinitely many values of $C$. The constructions use combinatorial arguments about the structure of the sumset.

title: erdos_C4_counterexample
content: **erdos_C4_counterexample** (Erdős 1980): Similarly, there exists a set $A$ with $r_A \leq 4$ that cannot be partitioned into pieces with $r < 4$.
mathContext: The case $C=4$ was proved alongside $C=3$ in [Er80e]. Erdős noted that his method extends to infinitely many $C$ but could not settle the question for all $C$, leaving that to Nešetřil and Rödl.

title: Nešetřil-Rödl Theorem (1985)
content:
**nesetril_rodl_theorem**: For ALL $C \geq 1$, there exists a 'bad' set $A$ with $r_A \leq C$ that cannot be partitioned into ANY number of pieces with $r_{A_i} < C$.

This is the complete negative answer to Problem #328.
mathContext: The proof [NeRo85] uses Ramsey-theoretic methods: interpret pairs summing to the same value as hyperedges in a hypergraph. A partition of $A$ is a vertex coloring; Ramsey theory guarantees a monochromatic subhypergraph with full convolution bound. The quantitative Ramsey bounds determine the minimum size of the counterexample.

title: erdos_newman_disproved
content:
**erdos_newman_disproved**: $\neg$ `erdos_newman_question`

The Erdős-Newman conjecture is FALSE. This follows from `nesetril_rodl_theorem` applied to any $C \geq 1$.
mathContext: The negation means: for some $C$, no uniform bound $t(C)$ suffices. In fact, the Nešetřil-Rödl theorem shows this for EVERY $C \geq 1$.

title: nesetril_rodl_strong
content: **nesetril_rodl_strong**: Even allowing $t$ to depend on $A$ itself (not just $C$), the answer is still NO. For every $C \geq 1$, there exist sets that resist partition into ANY finite number of pieces with smaller convolution.
mathContext: This strengthening rules out all partition strategies: not only uniform ones ($t$ depending on $C$) but also non-uniform ones ($t$ depending on $A$). The 'bad' sets produced by Ramsey theory have the property that every partition, no matter how fine, preserves the convolution bound in at least one piece.

title: sidon_case
content: **sidon_case**: Even Sidon sets ($C=2$) cannot always be partitioned into unique-sum sets ($r \leq 1$). This is the base case of the Nešetřil-Rödl theorem and the most concrete instance of the obstruction.
mathContext: Since $C=2$ is the smallest nontrivial case, this illustrates the phenomenon most vividly: a set where all pairwise sums are distinct still cannot be split into pieces where all sums are unique. The counterexample Sidon set must be constructed via Ramsey theory.

title: hasUniqueSums
content: **hasUniqueSums A**: $r_A(n) \leq 1$ for all $n$. Every integer has at most one representation as a sum of two elements from $A$. These sets are extremely sparse.
mathContext: Unique-sum sets satisfy $|A \cap [1,N]| = O(N^{1/3})$, much sparser than Sidon sets ($O(\sqrt{N})$). The property is hereditary (preserved by subsets), unlike bounded convolution for $C \geq 2$.

title: unique_sums_hereditary
content:
**unique_sums_hereditary**: If $A$ has unique sums and $B \subseteq A$, then $B$ also has unique sums.

This contrasts sharply with $C \geq 2$: Sidon is NOT hereditary in the partition sense (you can't always partition into unique-sum subsets).
mathContext: Heredity for $r_A \leq 1$ is immediate: if $B \subseteq A$, then any pair in $B$ summing to $n$ is also a pair in $A$ summing to $n$, so $r_B(n) \leq r_A(n) \leq 1$. This monotonicity fails for the partition question because partition pieces are not arbitrary subsets—they must cover all of $A$.
